messages.subject: knitr v0.9
messages.subject_clean: knitr v0.9
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm preparing the release of knitr v0.9, and I'll appreciate it if you
can test it before I upload it to CRAN. Please see the NEWS file for
all changes in the past three months:
https://github.com/yihui/knitr/blob/master/NEWS.md To install the
development version:

library(devtools)
install_github('evaluate', 'hadley')
install_github('knitr', 'yihui')

If there is one thing that might annoy you, it is \SweaveOpts{} and
\SweaveInput{} are going to disappear in the next version (either
v0.10 or v1.0); you are encouraged to use opts_chunk$set() and the
child option respectively, otherwise there will be a "penalty" of a
pause of 10 seconds when you knit a document; please pay attention to
the warning message in that case.

Two features that might interest you are the Shiny notebook and Rcpp support.

Thanks!

Regards,
Yihui

reproducible research.  As it stands, an *.Rnw file itself is not

tidy=FALSE. I do not know the real reason either, but you can
certainly use cat(..., sep = '') (the default value of sep is a
space), e.g.

>
>
>
> \textbf{Problem 1: Reading data into R}
> \begin{enumerate}
> \item Download the file "WomenStats.txt" from the course website and read
> this into R using
> read.table(), calling the new R object \verb+women+.
> \item What is the class and dimension of the object  \verb+women+?
>
>
> <<Problem1>>=
> #women<-read.table("WomenStats.txt", header=TRUE)
> xd1 <-
> "height  weight    age
> 58         115    33
> 59         117    34
> 60         120    37
> 61         123    31
> 62         126    31
> 63         129    34
> 64         132    31
> 65         135    39
> 66         139    35
> 67         142    34
> 68         146    34
> 69         150    36
> 70         154    33
> 71         159    30
> 72         164    37
> 71         160    NA
> 73         161    35"
> women <- read.table (textConnection(xd1), header=TRUE)
> class(women)
> dim(women)
> summary(women)
> @
>
> The \Rfunction{summary} is useful and it tells us that there is 1 missing
> values (NA) in the age column.  We will need to keep this in mind when we
> apply some of our statistical analyses on the data.
>
> \end{enumerate}
>
> \newpage
>
> \textbf{Problem 2: Matrix manipulations}
> \begin{enumerate}
> \item A new woman joined the study, she is 66" tall, 165 lbs and is 34
> years. Use \Rfunction{rbind} to append a row, containing her information to
> \verb+women+
>
> <<Problem2>>=
> newWoman<-c(66, 165,34)
> women<-rbind(women, newWoman)
> summary(women)
> @
>
>
>
> \item How many women have a weight under 140?
>
> You can simple get a vector of TRUE/FALSE by subsetting the women whose
> weight is less than 140.  The function \Rfunction{sum} can be used to
> quickly and easily count the number which are TRUE
>
> <<Problem2.1>>=
> women$weight<140
> sum(women$weight<140)
> @
>
>
> Alternative, create a vector and either tabulate it using \Rfunction{table}
>
> <<Problem2.1.1>>=
> table(women$weight<140)
>
> weight140 <- ifelse(women$weight<140, "under140", "over140")
> table(weight140)
> @
>
>
> \item What is the average height of women who weigh between 135 and 145
> pounds  (hint: first select the data and then find the mean. See the section
> in lecture 1 on Boolean terms and subsetting).
>
> First, lets subset the women who weight between 135 and 145 pounds and save
> this index.  Then select the height column and these rows from the matrix.
> I show a number of ways to do this below.
>
> <<Problem2.2.1>>=
> index<- women$weight>135 & women$weight<145
> index
> dim(women[index, ])
> @
>
>
> There are two women within this weight range. Now get the mean height of
> these two women.
>
> <<Problem2.2.2>>=
>
> mean(women[index, 1])
> mean(women[index, "height"])
> mean(women$height[index])
> @
>
>
> Another way to do this subsetting and selection is to use the function
> \Rfunction{subset}
> <<Problem2.2.3>>=
> help(subset)
> subWomen<-subset(women, subset=women$weight>135 & women$weight<145,
> select=height)
> print(subWomen)
> colMeans(subWomen)
> @
>
> \item Get help on the command \verb+colnames+
>
> <<Problem2.3>>=
> ?colnames
> help(colnames)
> @
>
> \item Change the rownames of \verb+women+ to the letters of the alphabet, eg
> "A", "B", "C", "D" etc
>
> <<Problem2.4>>=
> rownames(women) <- LETTERS[1:nrow(women)]
> @
>
> \item There is a correction to the women is row  D, her age should be 39.
> Change the age in row "D" to 39
>
>
> <<Problem2.5>>=
> women["D",]
> women["D", "age"] <-39
> women["D",]
> @
>
> \item Sort the matrix \verb+women+ by 'weight' and store the result in
> \verb+newWomen+
>
> <<Problem2.6>>=
> newWomen<-women[order(women$weight),]
> newWomen
> @
>
> \end{enumerate}
>
>
> \newpage
> \textbf{Problem 3: Using Apply}
>
>
> \begin{itemize}
> \item Use apply to generate a summary report, with the mean, median, sd of
> height, weight and age. \\ (Hint: use the \verb+apply+ function to get the
> \verb+mean+, \verb+median+ and \verb+sd+ of the columns and use \verb+rbind+
> to create a matrix with rownames; mean, median and sd).
>
> The \Rfunction{summary} only provides the mean, median, min, max and IQR of
> each column. To get the standard deviation, or variance we can use apply to
> get the \Rfunction{sd} \Rfunction{var} of each column.  By default it shows
> 6 decimal places.  For display purposes, we wish to see only 2 decimal
> places.
>
>
> <<Problem3>>=
> summary(women)
> @
>
>
> <<note3.1>>=
> colsd<-apply(women,2, sd)
> signif(colsd, digits=3)
> @
>
> Note: because of the NA (missing value) in Age, we get NA when we try to
> calculate the mean of age. So we need to give age an extra parameter so it
> knows how to deal with missing values.  We can tell mean to ignore missing
> values by setting the parameter na.rm =TRUE.  There are 2 ways to pass
> parameters to a function when using apply. One is writing it after the
> function call, there other is to create a function within the apply call.
>
> <<note3.2>>=
> apply(women,2, mean)
> apply(women,2, mean, na.rm=TRUE)
> apply(women,2, function(x) mean(x,na.rm=TRUE))
> @
>
> We could pass more than one argument to the function using either of these
> approaches. For example if we also wished to trim 10% of observation from
> each end of the mean.
>
> <<note3.3>>=
> apply(women,2, mean, na.rm=TRUE, trim=0.1)
> apply(women,2, function(x) mean(x,na.rm=TRUE, trim=.1))
> @
>
>
> So here is the function
>
> <<Function3.4>>=
>
> mySummary<-function(df) {
>     colMeans<-apply(df,2, mean, na.rm=TRUE)
>     colMedians<-apply(df,2, median, na.rm=TRUE)
>     colSDs<-apply(df,2, sd, na.rm=TRUE)
>     res<-rbind(mean=colMeans, median=colMedians, sd=colSDs)
>     res<-apply(res,2, signif, digits = 3)
>     return(res)
>     }
>
> mySummary(women)
> @
>
>
> \end{itemize}
>
> \textbf{Problem 4: Loops and Functions}
> \begin{enumerate}
>
> \item  Write a function to calculate BMI. The function should have 2 inputs;
> weight(lb) and height(in) and should return one value; BMI.
>
>
> <<Problem4.1>>=
>
> bmi<-function(weight, height) {
>     bmi<- (weight/height^2)*703
>     bmi<-  round(bmi, 2)
>     return(bmi)
>     }
>
> bmi(weight=150, height=65)
> bmi(150, 65)
> @
>
>
>
>
> \item  Do the women have a BMI within the recommend range ? (Normal
> $\approx$  18.5-24.9)?
>
> Here is how we would calculate the BMI of every woman.
> <<Problem4.2.1>>=
> bmi(women$weight, women$height)
> cat(paste("The BMI of woman", rownames(women),"is", bmi(women$weight,
> women$height), "\n"))
>
> @
>
>
> To test the output of the calculation to see if it falls within normal
> range.  We will do this using a few alternative approaches (see below)
>
> Solution I would use.
>
> <<Problem4.3.3>>=
> bmiRes<-bmi(women$weight, women$height)
> women<-cbind(women, bmi=bmiRes)
> res<-sum(women$bmi<18.5 | women$bmi>24.9)
> print(paste("The number of women with BMI values outside the normal range
> is:", res))
> @
>
>
>
> Alternative 1 : Using a For loop.  This is not the optimal solution, but I
> include it here so you would see how you could write a For loop
> <<Problem4.3.1>>=
>
> for (i in 1:nrow(women))  {
>      bmiRes<-bmi(women$weight[i], women$height[i])
>      out<-ifelse(bmiRes<18.5 | bmiRes>24.9, "Not normal", "normal")
>      print(out)
>      }
> @
>
> Alternative 2
> Saving the output to a vector.  Again using a For loop.  This is not the
> optimal solution, but I include it here so you would see how to add values
> to an empty vector when using a For loop
>
> <<Problem4.3.2>>=
>
> BMIres<-vector()
>
> for (i in 1:nrow(women))  {
>      bmiRes[i]<-bmi(women$weight[i], women$height[i])
>      }
>
> print(bmiRes)
> print(paste("Number of abnormal bmi values: ", sum(bmiRes<18.5 |
> bmiRes>24.9)))
> @
>
> Taking the vector above, but printing the result using an ifelse conditional
> test
>
> <<Problem4.3.3>>=
> res<- ifelse(bmiRes<18.5 | bmiRes>24.9, "abnormal BMI", "normal BMI")
> table(res)
> \end{enumerate}
> @
>
> \end{enumerate}
>
> \end{document}

> > \verb+women+
> >
> > <<Problem2>>=
> > newWoman<-c(66, 165,34)
> > women<-rbind(women, newWoman)
> > summary(women)
> > @
> >
> >
> >
> > \item How many women have a weight under 140?
> >
> > You can simple get a vector of TRUE/FALSE by subsetting the women whose
> > weight is less than 140.  The function \Rfunction{sum} can be used to
> > quickly and easily count the number which are TRUE
> >
> > <<Problem2.1>>=
> > women$weight<140
> > sum(women$weight<140)
> > @
> >
> >
> > Alternative, create a vector and either tabulate it using \Rfunction{table}
> >
> > <<Problem2.1.1>>=
> > table(women$weight<140)
> >
> > weight140 <- ifelse(women$weight<140, "under140", "over140")
> > table(weight140)
> > @
> >
> >
> > \item What is the average height of women who weigh between 135 and 145
> > pounds  (hint: first select the data and then find the mean. See the section
> > in lecture 1 on Boolean terms and subsetting).
> >
> > First, lets subset the women who weight between 135 and 145 pounds and save
> > this index.  Then select the height column and these rows from the matrix.
> > I show a number of ways to do this below.
> >
> > <<Problem2.2.1>>=
> > index<- women$weight>135 & women$weight<145
> > index
> > dim(women[index, ])
> > @
> >
> >
> > There are two women within this weight range. Now get the mean height of
> > these two women.
> >
> > <<Problem2.2.2>>=
> >
> > mean(women[index, 1])
> > mean(women[index, "height"])
> > mean(women$height[index])
> > @
> >
> >
> > Another way to do this subsetting and selection is to use the function
> > \Rfunction{subset}
> > <<Problem2.2.3>>=
> > help(subset)
> > subWomen<-subset(women, subset=women$weight>135 & women$weight<145,
> > select=height)
> > print(subWomen)
> > colMeans(subWomen)
> > @
> >
> > \item Get help on the command \verb+colnames+
> >
> > <<Problem2.3>>=
> > ?colnames
> > help(colnames)
> > @
> >
> > \item Change the rownames of \verb+women+ to the letters of the alphabet, eg
> > "A", "B", "C", "D" etc
> >
> > <<Problem2.4>>=
> > rownames(women) <- LETTERS[1:nrow(women)]
> > @
> >
> > \item There is a correction to the women is row  D, her age should be 39.
> > Change the age in row "D" to 39
> >
> >
> > <<Problem2.5>>=
> > women["D",]
> > women["D", "age"] <-39
> > women["D",]
> > @
> >
> > \item Sort the matrix \verb+women+ by 'weight' and store the result in
> > \verb+newWomen+
> >
> > <<Problem2.6>>=
> > newWomen<-women[order(women$weight),]
> > newWomen
> > @
> >
> > \end{enumerate}
> >
> >
> > \newpage
> > \textbf{Problem 3: Using Apply}
> >
> >
> > \begin{itemize}
> > \item Use apply to generate a summary report, with the mean, median, sd of
> > height, weight and age. \\ (Hint: use the \verb+apply+ function to get the
> > \verb+mean+, \verb+median+ and \verb+sd+ of the columns and use \verb+rbind+
> > to create a matrix with rownames; mean, median and sd).
> >
> > The \Rfunction{summary} only provides the mean, median, min, max and IQR of
> > each column. To get the standard deviation, or variance we can use apply to
> > get the \Rfunction{sd} \Rfunction{var} of each column.  By default it shows
> > 6 decimal places.  For display purposes, we wish to see only 2 decimal
> > places.
> >
> >
> > <<Problem3>>=
> > summary(women)
> > @
> >
> >
> > <<note3.1>>=
> > colsd<-apply(women,2, sd)
> > signif(colsd, digits=3)
> > @
> >
> > Note: because of the NA (missing value) in Age, we get NA when we try to
> > calculate the mean of age. So we need to give age an extra parameter so it
> > knows how to deal with missing values.  We can tell mean to ignore missing
> > values by setting the parameter na.rm =TRUE.  There are 2 ways to pass
> > parameters to a function when using apply. One is writing it after the
> > function call, there other is to create a function within the apply call.
> >
> > <<note3.2>>=
> > apply(women,2, mean)
> > apply(women,2, mean, na.rm=TRUE)
> > apply(women,2, function(x) mean(x,na.rm=TRUE))
> > @
> >
> > We could pass more than one argument to the function using either of these
> > approaches. For example if we also wished to trim 10% of observation from
> > each end of the mean.
> >
> > <<note3.3>>=
> > apply(women,2, mean, na.rm=TRUE, trim=0.1)
> > apply(women,2, function(x) mean(x,na.rm=TRUE, trim=.1))
> > @
> >
> >
> > So here is the function
> >
> > <<Function3.4>>=
> >
> > mySummary<-function(df) {
> >     colMeans<-apply(df,2, mean, na.rm=TRUE)
> >     colMedians<-apply(df,2, median, na.rm=TRUE)
> >     colSDs<-apply(df,2, sd, na.rm=TRUE)
> >     res<-rbind(mean=colMeans, median=colMedians, sd=colSDs)
> >     res<-apply(res,2, signif, digits = 3)
> >     return(res)
> >     }
> >
> > mySummary(women)
> > @
> >
> >
> > \end{itemize}
> >
> > \textbf{Problem 4: Loops and Functions}
> > \begin{enumerate}
> >
> > \item  Write a function to calculate BMI. The function should have 2 inputs;
> > weight(lb) and height(in) and should return one value; BMI.
> >
> >
> > <<Problem4.1>>=
> >
> > bmi<-function(weight, height) {
> >     bmi<- (weight/height^2)*703
> >     bmi<-  round(bmi, 2)
> >     return(bmi)
> >     }
> >
> > bmi(weight=150, height=65)
> > bmi(150, 65)
> > @
> >
> >
> >
> >
> > \item  Do the women have a BMI within the recommend range ? (Normal
> > $\approx$  18.5-24.9)?
> >
> > Here is how we would calculate the BMI of every woman.
> > <<Problem4.2.1>>=
> > bmi(women$weight, women$height)
> > cat(paste("The BMI of woman", rownames(women),"is", bmi(women$weight,
> > women$height), "\n"))
> >
> > @
> >
> >
> > To test the output of the calculation to see if it falls within normal
> > range.  We will do this using a few alternative approaches (see below)
> >
> > Solution I would use.
> >
> > <<Problem4.3.3>>=
> > bmiRes<-bmi(women$weight, women$height)
> > women<-cbind(women, bmi=bmiRes)
> > res<-sum(women$bmi<18.5 | women$bmi>24.9)
> > print(paste("The number of women with BMI values outside the normal range
> > is:", res))
> > @
> >
> >
> >
> > Alternative 1 : Using a For loop.  This is not the optimal solution, but I
> > include it here so you would see how you could write a For loop
> > <<Problem4.3.1>>=
> >
> > for (i in 1:nrow(women))  {
> >      bmiRes<-bmi(women$weight[i], women$height[i])
> >      out<-ifelse(bmiRes<18.5 | bmiRes>24.9, "Not normal", "normal")
> >      print(out)
> >      }
> > @
> >
> > Alternative 2
> > Saving the output to a vector.  Again using a For loop.  This is not the
> > optimal solution, but I include it here so you would see how to add values
> > to an empty vector when using a For loop
> >
> > <<Problem4.3.2>>=
> >
> > BMIres<-vector()
> >
> > for (i in 1:nrow(women))  {
> >      bmiRes[i]<-bmi(women$weight[i], women$height[i])
> >      }
> >
> > print(bmiRes)
> > print(paste("Number of abnormal bmi values: ", sum(bmiRes<18.5 |
> > bmiRes>24.9)))
> > @
> >
> > Taking the vector above, but printing the result using an ifelse conditional
> > test
> >
> > <<Problem4.3.3>>=
> > res<- ifelse(bmiRes<18.5 | bmiRes>24.9, "abnormal BMI", "normal BMI")
> > table(res)
> > \end{enumerate}
> > @
> >
> > \end{enumerate}
> >
> > \end{document}
